fatal_errors: The proposed copper coating plus compression-plasma-flow treatment is a surface-modification route and does not reconstruct the target intervention of liquid-metal dealloying a directionally segregated WTaVTi precursor in molten Cu.

The hypothesis extrapolates near-surface W(Cu) formation to elimination of bulk voids and phase separation in an entire W–Cu joint without evidence that the approximately 100 microsecond treatment can modify a macroscopic interconnected structure.

Improved thermal conductivity, interfacial strength, and mechanical durability are asserted even though the cited evidence primarily supports microstructural formation and limited helium-ion radiation-response observations, not those bulk properties.
explanation: The hypothesis addresses the general W–Cu fusion-material problem and proposes a literature-supported alternative involving copper coating and pulsed plasma processing. It is nevertheless unrelated to the hidden target's selective liquid-metal dealloying of Ti/V-rich channels in a directionally solidified WTaVTi alloy at 1200 °C for 96 h. It therefore misses the bicontinuous RHEA–Cu architecture, W-rich passivating interlayer, selective Ti–Cu exchange mechanism, temperature-dependent conductivity result, and carefully limited 25 keV He+ screening. The proposed experiment includes relevant microstructural, thermal, irradiation, and mechanical comparisons, but the baseline is broad, simulated service conditions are insufficiently specified, and the 20% criterion is arbitrary. Evidence E2 supports CPF-induced near-surface W–Cu phases and some helium-ion resistance, but not uniform bulk densification or preserved joint durability; the proposed 25–35 J/cm² range also only partly overlaps the cited 35–55 J/cm² range. Because the intervention is largely restated from E2 rather than newly derived, novelty is limited.
